newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone prepares to celebrate peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone prepares to celebrate peace deal.

text.p: Sierra Leone prepared to celebrate the signing in Ivory Coast on Friday of a peace deal to end more than five years of civil war with state radio assuring the nation that the ceremony would go ahead.

But in Ivory Coast, where rebel leader Foday Sankoh returned on Wednesday after talks with his fighters in the bush and President Henri Konan Bedie was returning from a visit to Europe, there was no official word on the ceremony.

State radio in Sierra Leone said on Thursday that the government of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah was calling on churches and mosques to ring their bells or sound a signal to the faithful to welcome the return of peace.
At noon -- the signing time -- all ships in port, all cars and trucks throughout the West African nation should sound their horns, it added.

Traditional rulers from rebel-held areas in the east said on Wednesday Sankoh's fighters had demanded international monitors to guarantee their safety and disbanding of civil defence units made up of Kamajor traditional hunters before any signing.

The Kamajors had been attacking rebel positions across the nation and the truce extended by Tejan Kabbah and Sankoh in talks in Ivory Coast in April had looked more and more fragile prior to the latest peace developments.
But government sources said on Friday that Sankoh had told Ivory Coast he was prepared to sign on Friday as scheduled.
U.N. sources close to the peace process said that an Ivorian presidential jet would take Tejan Kabbah and a cross-section of Sierra Leonians to Ivory Coast for the signing.
Sankoh told Reuters in Ivory Coast's commercial capital on Wednesday he had had "fruitful" talks with his guerrillas back in the Sierra Leone jungle on a mandate to sign the accord.

But he declined any comment on whether he actually got a mandate or if indeed there will be an accord this week, saying he has to first consult the Ivorian mediators. "I can't say anything until the next 72 hours. I am waiting for the foreign minister and president of Ivory Coast," he said.
Kabbah, who took office in March after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule, earlier threatened the military option if Sankoh did not agree to peace by December 1.
The civil war in Sierra Leone, a former British colony, has killed at least 10,000 people, according to official estimates.
The rebels launched a low-level guerrilla campaign from the border with Liberia in March 1991. A 1992 army coup failed to bring a military solution.
Rebels who held 17 foreign hostages for months disrupted the country's mainstay bauxite, rutile, diamonds and gold mining industry by forcing foreign-owned mines to close or cut back.
By early 1995 rebels were attacking close to the capital. The government brought in mercenaries from South African firm Executive Outcomes and retook the initiative.
Differences over the presence of foreign troops -- Nigerians, Guineans and the South Africans -- blocked a deal.
Police said on Thursday more than 100 traditional drumming groups had applied to dance in the streets and they had been given special permission despite the late requests.
"They will be celebrating the end of the war. All traditional dance clubs and masquerades will be free to occupy the streets of Freetown," a spokesman said.
